name: Polyquaternium-10
lead: Polyquaternium-10 (PQ-10) is the INCI name for quaternized hydroxyethyl cellulose, a cellulose-derived polymer carrying positively charged quaternary ammonium groups.[1] It belongs to the polyquaternium family, of which at least 40 members have been approved.[1]

It is used in shampoos and conditioners, where cationic polymers are described as providing conditioning, smoothing, easier combing and creamier lather.[2] It has also been studied in hydrogels, drug-delivery matrices and sensors.[3][4]

paras: A 2000 review of conditioning polymers in shampoos described cationic polymers as important for conditioning and smoothing, and noted the move from 2-in-1 to 3-in-1 shampoos.[2] Their positive charge lets them bind to hair and skin and helps neutralise the negative charge on hair proteins and in shampoos.[1]

PQ-10 has been cross-linked into hydrogels characterised as pH- and ion-sensitive drug-delivery systems,[3] studied with surfactants and thickeners,[5] and used in an ionic hydrogel for flexible thermal sensors.[4] These are not appearance applications.
No studies found. A registered phase 2 trial of probiotic-containing hair products (NCT04566549, 21 participants) is not a study of PQ-10.[6]

card.summary: Cationic cellulose polymer that coats hair in shampoos and conditioners; a background ingredient with no direct trials.
card.note: No hair-specific clinical or safety data found in the reviewed sources.

quick.overview:
Polyquaternium-10 is a modified cellulose with positive charges, used in shampoos and conditioners. Formulation literature credits cationic polymers with easier combing, smoother hair and better lather.

It is an ingredient rather than a treatment; no trials of it on hair were found.
quick.mechanism: Its positive charge attracts it to negatively charged hair, where it deposits as a thin conditioning film.
quick.risks: The reviewed sources report no specific safety findings for PQ-10 on hair or skin.
